p: Teo told it all at his kitchen table. A big man grabbed him in the bar, and their father hit the man first. Out back the man had their father pinned on the tailgate, and Teo hit him once in the face with a flashlight.

Their father drove him to a gas station by the on ramp, where the register clock said five after eleven, and threw the receipt away. He dropped the flashlight off a bridge and took Teo to their grandmother's, and she said he'd been there all night.
The autopsy puts Teo's swing above the eye, a cut that had no part in the death. The fracture at the back of the skull killed him, and a pathologist says it fits an object or a curb.
Teo gave the lab his own DNA, and in August he told Ana he'll testify. Their father says no.
That night, on the phone, Dani moved her knight to the middle of the board.
Ana Brennan. In a courtroom for Dani's father again, at last.
Teo Ruiz. He's going to testify.
Luis Ruiz. Still Wednesdays at seven, and he owes Dani a move.
Meredith Sloane. The chief deputy district attorney. You've heard her once, on Ana's speaker in May.
Martin Esquibel. The Adams County district judge hearing the motion.
Consuelo Baca. The eyewitness from across the lot.
Celeste Abeyta. A defense lawyer. Hers is the name Ana wrote down for Teo.

Thursday, August 19, she was thirty five. Nobody at the office knew it, and she didn't tell anybody. She ate lunch at her desk over somebody else's motion to suppress, half a turkey sandwich and an apple, and at ten after two her phone buzzed against the stapler with Ana's name on it.
It came, Ana said. I'm not reading it to you over the phone. Come when you're done there.

She put the other half of the sandwich in her drawer, told Joel she was taking the afternoon, and caught the 2:31 out Colfax. A man across the aisle was eating sunflower seeds out of a paper cup and spitting the shells back into it, one at a time, the whole way.

The laundromat was half empty in the middle of the afternoon, and the stairs smelled like it anyway. Upstairs Ana had two stapled pages face down on the desk with her hand flat on top of them, like they might get up and leave.

The report was two pages with the state seal at the top and a case number she knew by heart. Ana turned it over and slid it across the desk, and then she got up and went to the window and looked down at the bus bench, so she wouldn't be watching Dani read.

Colorado Bureau of Investigation, forensic DNA report, summary of results. Item 7. Fingernail scrapings and clippings, right and left hands of Travis Hensley, collected at autopsy, October 28, 2007. Reference samples compared: Travis Hensley (blood standard, 2007). Luis Ruiz (2027). Teo Ruiz (collected July 16, 2027). Right hand. A mixture of DNA from two people. Travis Hensley is included as a contributor. Luis Ruiz is included as a contributor. Teo Ruiz is excluded. Left hand. A mixture of DNA from two people. Travis Hensley is included as a contributor. The other contributor is male and is designated Unknown Male 1. Luis Ruiz and Teo Ruiz are excluded as the source of Unknown Male 1. The profile of Unknown Male 1 was searched in the state and national DNA databases. No match was found. These results identify whose DNA is present. They do not establish when, or by what kind of contact, any of it was deposited.

She read it twice. Right hand, her father. She'd told Ana in May that his would be under there, and why, across this desk. I saw his neck that Sunday. Now it had a state seal over it and a staple in the corner.
All those years on a shelf in a property room in Commerce City, Ana said to the window, and it comes back with something on both hands. Pick me the line I carry into that courtroom. I get one.

The left hand, she says. A second man, and he isn't Pa or Teo. Ana turns around from the window and says that's the one. She reads the left hand out loud to the room, and then she reads the last line too, the one about when and how, because Meredith will read it out loud if she doesn't. In 2008 the State told a jury that one man fought Travis Hensley that night and the man in red was him, and under his other hand there was somebody that jury never heard about. Ana writes LEFT HAND on an index card. The card goes in her shirt pocket, behind the pencil.

Strengthen a passage claim. The motion says the State's case broke when it assumed the man who fought Travis was the only man who had hold of him. A second male profile under his nails, excluded as Luis's and as Teo's, is new evidence of another man in contact with him. The report's last line limits it: it can't say when.

She drove over to Teo's at nine without calling. Teo was out in the carport in a lawn chair, Sprite by his boot, string lights from March over his head not plugged in. Bianca's car was gone. The only light in the house was Lupe's turtle. She sat down on the side door step next to the charcoal and told him all of it. Pa under one hand, some other man under the other one, him under neither.

He listened with his elbows on his knees. When she was done he said excluded back to her, slow, the way he'd read a part number off a box, and then he said, So it wasn't me. That's what that means, right? It wasn't me.
She'd read that word about fifty times on the bus home, between Federal and her stop, with the report folded in half on top of the prep book. Whatever she told him it meant, he was going to keep.
It's like no prints on a glass, Teo. You didn't hold it. You were in the room.

I never touched him with my hands, he says. Just the flashlight. She says she knows. She says she knows, and that's what the glass is for. He turns the can around on his knee a few times. But somebody had hold of him. Some other guy. She says somebody did. The paper doesn't say when. He nods at the dark yard for a while, and then he gets up and plugs the string lights in, which he hasn't done since March.

Analogy. Exclusion says his DNA isn't among what was under the nails. Like prints missing from a glass, it shows he didn't leave that trace. Whether he was in the room is a question the glass can't answer, and here only Teo's own word answers it.
Tuesday, August 24, there was a sticky note on the corner of Ana's desk in her own pencil. CELESTE ABEYTA, and a number under it.

Your brother's lawyer, Ana said. She called me at eight this morning. It's the name I wrote him in July. He carried it around in his wallet for a month and then he called it. She leaned back and the chair said so. Your brother isn't my client. He never was. Now he's got somebody whose client he is, and that's the best thing that's happened in this case since May.

Celeste had asked her one thing, Ana said, what Teo had to lose, and Ana had told her that was Celeste's to answer and not hers. Dani didn't ask what the answer was. As far as anybody would say out loud, it wasn't a cell. It was Pa, and keeping still since he was ten, and whatever a man has left after he says in a courtroom that he hit somebody in the head with a steel flashlight when he was ten.
And from now to the thirteenth, whatever he says to you, I hear it the next morning, Ana said. Same as July. That part worked fine.

She took the card out of her shirt pocket, the one she'd shown Dani in March with the four lines on it, gone soft at the corners from riding around against her pencil all summer. Dani read it again anyway. The jury never heard it. He and his lawyer couldn't have known it, with reasonable care. It's about what happened, not only about whether somebody's believable. It would probably bring an acquittal. Ana set it on the desk between them and asked what it did with Teo on the witness stand, one line at a time, the way she'd have asked it of a stranger.

Line two stops him, Dani says, because Pa always knew, but he can still help the judge read the DNA. Ana says that's it. He isn't new. Meredith's going to say so before her coffee gets cold, and I'm going to stand up and agree with her. What's new is under that left hand, Ana says, and Teo's how a judge reads it: why their father lied to Gene, why his skin's under the other hand, where the truck was at five after eleven. She writes TEO on the back of the card, small.

Apply the principle. Walk Teo through all four lines. He fails line two, since Luis always knew, so his account can't be the new evidence. That doesn't keep him off the stand. The new evidence is the DNA, and his testimony bears on what it would mean to a jury.
Teo had called her that week, late, from the truck. She's seven on the fourth. We're telling her Sunday. You're coming. He hung up before she could answer.

That Sunday, the twenty ninth, they told Lupe after lunch. Bianca kept a hand on the back of Lupe's chair. Teo had a work order in his shirt pocket with some of it written on the back, and he never took it out. Lupe chewed and listened and asked one thing, if he was the one who sent the knight, and Dani said he was. Can he come to my party? Teo said not this one, mija. She asked could she have his crusts.
Around four he walked Dani out to her car and stood there with his keys. Help me with it, he said. Be her. Ask me how she's gonna ask it.

It was all true, what he'd told her in July. A true thing doesn't get less true because you go over it twice with your sister in a driveway, so going over it couldn't hurt. She got that far, standing on his oil stain.
You told Ana why yourself. If I help, you won't know which part's yours.

He turns the keys over a couple more times. Yeah, he says. I did say that. She tells him she'll be right behind the rail the whole time and she won't help him with one word of it, not one. He gets the truck door open and stands in it. Then don't look at me up there. She says she'll look at her shoes. Those shoes, he says, and gets in, and backs the truck out so she can get out.

Flaw. The argument assumes that because the account is true, going over it can't change it. But practice changes what a witness says and how, and then nobody, him included, can tell which words came from the night and which came from the carport. A true story doesn't protect the telling.

Thursday, September 9, five days after Lupe turned seven in the paper crown from March, Ana had both reports out side by side on the desk, the 2007 autopsy and Solberg's letter, with a pencil line down the margin of each where the word separate came up.

Solberg's Monday afternoon, she said. Meredith's going to read her the 2007 report out loud and ask her if she agrees with it. Your brother's going to be sitting there when she answers. Put these next to each other.

Two lines, side by side. 2007: The laceration above the left eyebrow is a separate, superficial injury and is non-contributory. 2027: I can't tell from the record which injury came first or how much time separated them. He lived for some hours after he reached the hospital, so the bruising doesn't settle the order.
Ana tapped the lower one with the eraser end of her pencil and asked what it did with the first one's word.

Took up the question and couldn't close it, Dani says, and Ana writes that in the margin. Two injuries, the old report says, and stops. Solberg asks the next question, which one first and how long between, and then says the body can't tell her. And your brother's going to sit there and hear a doctor say she doesn't know which came first, Ana says. He does. He's the only one in that room who does.

Comparative passages. The 2007 report says only that the injuries were separate. Solberg's review takes up what that word leaves open, the order and the time between them, and says the record can't settle it. The second document asks the first one's unasked question and marks where the evidence stops.

Friday on the bus she read the reading Ana had sent her home with. Students in Seattle in 1974 who heard smashed instead of hit and remembered broken glass that was never in the film. Two psychologists in 2017 who said the first test of a memory, done right, tells you more than the courts thought. It wasn't so she'd know what to say, Ana had told her. It was so she'd know what Meredith was doing when she asked. They'd brought her father down to the county jail in Brighton that same morning.

He'd called the three Wednesdays since from Sterling and left her knight where it was. On the second she told him Lupe knew about him now, and that Lupe had asked if he could come to her party. Tell her next one, he said, and then he talked about the heat.

Sunday, September 12, at seven, her phone rang from a number she didn't know, and the recording named the county jail instead of Sterling. She took it on the step anyway. It was where she took his calls.
They bus you down in a cage with a window the size of a paperback, he said. I saw some corn. I saw Fort Morgan go by. Then I saw a wall.
She told him first, before the board. Teo was getting up there tomorrow. Whatever her father said, to her, to Ana, to anybody.
I said no, mija. Twice. I told Brennan. Teo told Ana you don't get a vote, Pa. You don't.

Nothing on the line. A TV somewhere behind him, a different one from the tier's, and a man asking somebody for a pencil. She'd been working up to the rest of it since the carport. It was the only move she had.
TEO'S WORD, she'd written on the card in July. The pump at 11:05, the bridge, Abuela's porch. Nobody alive had seen any of it but Teo and the man on this phone.
She'll say he's your son, Pa, and nobody else saw that lot. Just you.

He's quiet long enough that she checks the screen. Then, low: A son would say anything. That's what she'll say, Pa. Not Ronnie, who never looked down. Not Consuelo, who heard a boy and saw her own kitchen in the glass.

Weaken. Teo's account rests on Teo alone, and Teo is Luis's son. The strongest attack gives his testimony a reason to exist whether or not it's true: a son wants his father home. It doesn't prove he's lying. It's a hole only another witness can close.

She said the rest of it before the minute warning, because there wasn't going to be another call. He can tell them he swung, Pa. He can't tell them why. He was ten. He was looking at the man. The board was right in front of her and she didn't look at it. Only one person can tell a judge why. It isn't Teo, and it isn't me.

With the warning going he gave her his move. Knight out, the square, letter and number, the way he'd taught her. Then the line went dead. At the kitchen table she found the square and set his knight on it, facing hers across the middle of the board. If she wanted to trade, she could. He'd answered it. He hadn't said what else he'd answered.
At half past eight she drove to Federal, because Ana had said to come by if he called, and the light was on upstairs. Ana had two cards out on the desk, one for each side.

Ana's two cards. MEREDITH: THE JURY KNEW HE FOUGHT HIM. THE DNA SAYS HE FOUGHT HIM. ANOTHER MAN IN A PACKED BAR ON A SERIES NIGHT TOUCHED HIM. THAT'S A CROWD BRUSHING PAST HIM, NOT A MAN WHO HAD HOLD OF HIM, AND NOT AN ATTACKER. ANA: THE STATE NEEDED ONE MAN TO HAVE HAD HOLD OF HIM THAT NIGHT. THERE WERE TWO. A JURY THAT HEARD THAT PROBABLY DOESN'T CONVICT ON A JACKET.
Ten minutes each in the morning, Ana said. Where's the fight? Not the case. The fight on these two cards.
Whether the second profile means another man had hold of him.
That's the whole hearing, Ana says. She says it's a crowd. I say a man had hold of him. Same two pages from the lab, read two ways. She draws a line from one card to the other.
Point at issue. Meredith says the second profile is ordinary contact in a crowd. I say it shows a second man had hold of him. One of us says yes and the other says no, about the same thing.

At eleven, with her bag packed, Ana opened the top drawer and took the opinion out and laid it open on the desk to page eleven. The soft copy, the coffee ring. The small circled 1 in the margin beside the one sentence.

I put that there the week after, she said. The night after a girl sat across from me and asked what they had to believe. Not before I filed. After. The brief had it ninth. She looked at the chair Dani was sitting in, the one across the desk. That chair was in my office at the division. I brought it with me when I left. You sat in it with your mother's car keys in your lap and asked me what they had to believe. I knew. I wrote eight other things.

Dani had the keys before she had anything else. Ma's ring, with the grocery store tags and the brass tab from the hospital lot. She'd held them so hard she had the marks after, all the way home in Ma's car. She'd kept the no all these years. She hadn't kept the face.

I didn't know it was you, Dani said. I know, Ana said. She was looking at the chair, not at her. You came up those stairs in November with that transcript and sat down in it like it was any chair. You never answered me. Ana put the pencil down. I've been answering you since that night. Then she closed the opinion and put it back in the drawer, face up this time, and told Dani to go home and sleep, and that tomorrow she'd sit behind the rail and help nobody.
At home she hung her keys on the hook under Ma's lanyard and stood in the dark kitchen a while before she went up.

On Friday Joel had signed her leave slip for Monday and Tuesday without reading it, then read it, and added Wednesday in his own hand. Nobody's any good the day after, he said. And the schools are opening applications. Some already have. Don't spend Wednesday here.

Monday, September 13, the lot at the Justice Center in Brighton was already full at a quarter past eight, and the line at the metal detector went out the door, and the man in front of her had to walk back to his car with a pocketknife. By the elevators Meredith Sloane stopped Ana with a coffee in each hand and gave her one, and Dani was two steps behind and heard all of it. He walked up your stairs and gave my investigator the inside of his cheek before anybody knew a thing. I've wondered since July. Why? Ana told her to ask him. Meredith said she wouldn't be asking him that on the stand, and pushed three.

Shannon Hensley was already in the second row on the State's side when they went in, by herself, with her purse on her knees and both hands on the clasp, looking at the seal on the wall over the bench like she was reading it.

A deputy brought her father in the side door and sat him down next to Ana, and he turned around in his chair and found Teo in the front row next to Celeste Abeyta and her legal pad. The last time the two of them were in one room was Ma's viewing, eleven years back. Teo looked back at him till the deputy said something and Pa turned around to the front.

They each did their ten minutes, more or less what was on Ana's cards, and then Meredith stayed standing and said she had one more thing, in case anybody meant to call the son's account new, or the boy in the lot. If the son was in that lot, his father brought him there and drove him away and has known it every day since. Whatever the son says, it isn't new.

Ana got up with the March card in her hand, her thumb on line two, the one about what the defense couldn't have known, and said the People were right about that, and Judge Esquibel wrote something on his pad. Noted. Then what's new is the report. Ana said yes, Judge, the report, and sat back down.

Meredith sits too, with the face of somebody who brought an umbrella and found the sun out. Line two on the March card was settled in about six minutes by the clock over the door, and the rest of the day was going to be the left hand and the people who could tell a judge what it meant.

Point of agreement. Meredith says that if the son was in the lot, his father has known it all along, so whatever the son says isn't new. I told the court the People were right about that. A concession is a point of agreement in the speaker's own words.

Ana called Teo first. He went up past the rail in his good shirt, the blue one from Ma's viewing, and Celeste Abeyta slid down to the end of the front row so he'd be able to see her, and he put his hand up for the oath a little too high, like a kid in school.

Twenty five minutes. Twice he got the order wrong, the Sprites and then the tailgate, and went back and fixed it himself without anybody asking him to. Ana let him. The court reporter asked him once to slow down. In the lot part he said Papi. He just said it, in front of the judge and the deputy and Travis Hensley's sister, and went on to the truck.
Dani looked at her shoes for most of it, the brown ones with the scuffed toe, like she'd told him she would.

Meredith didn't raise her voice once. Was he ten that night. Yes, ma'am. Had he believed for twenty years that he'd killed Travis Hensley. Yes. Had his father been in prison most of that time. Yes, and he looked at his hands on the rail when he said it. Nobody saw your father at that gas station but you. Nobody saw that bridge but you. Nobody has ever found a flashlight. He said no, ma'am. Last she asked if he loved his father. Teo looked over at their father's table, the first time he'd looked there since he put his hand up. Yes, ma'am. Meredith said she had nothing further.
Esquibel gave them ten minutes before redirect. Ana came to the rail and bent down so only Dani would hear. I get one question, she said. Which?
When you gave your sample on July sixteenth, what did you think it would show?

Ana asks it. Teo looks at Celeste, and then at nobody. That it was me, he says. Under there. I thought it was going to say it was me. Ana asks who sealed it. A man from the district attorney's office, he says, at Ana's desk, and they both signed. Meredith writes something down. She'd asked why in the hall that morning. Now it's in the record, in his voice.

Strengthen. Meredith's attack is that a son would say anything to free his father. A son who hands the State his own DNA while he still believes it will show he killed a man isn't shaping evidence for anybody. It was fixed in place, by the State's own investigator, before anyone knew what it would show.

After lunch Ana called Dr. Solberg, who wore a gray suit and reading glasses on a cord and answered every question as if somebody she respected had asked it. For forty minutes she said what her letter said, in nearly the same words. The fracture at the back of the skull killed him. Its features fit a blow from an object or the back of his head striking a hard edge, like a curb, and the findings alone couldn't tell her which. The cut above the eye was real and shallow and played no part in his death. She couldn't say which injury came first or how long came between them. When Ana asked whether the cut could have put him on the ground, she said nothing in the record showed that it did.

Meredith's cross was short. She read the opinion paragraph of the 2007 report out loud, slowly, to its last words. The manner of death is homicide. Doctor, your letter says a curb. Are you telling this court Mr. Hensley fell? Solberg said she wasn't telling the court anything the findings didn't. A blow or a curb, and she couldn't choose, and wouldn't. And a steel flashlight could have made that fracture. An object could have, Solberg said. She'd never seen the object. Nobody has, Meredith said, and sat down.

In the front row Teo had gone still, the way he went still under a bus when he heard something he didn't like. Dani knew what he'd just heard. She also knew where his swing had landed. Above the eye. She'd told him so at his own kitchen table.

Driving home down 85 at six, Dani held the two pages in her head side by side, the way Ana had laid them on the desk. Homicide on one. A curb on the other. For about a second in that courtroom she'd thought the two of them couldn't both be right.

Blunt force injury of the head, the old report says. Not an object. Not a curb. Anything hard that meets a head fast. Solberg didn't take back a word of it. She said blunt force could have been a thing in somebody's hand or the edge of a curb, and that was as far as fourteen photographs would take her. A man knocked over backward onto a curb by somebody's swing is still a homicide. Meredith had read the two pages like they were arguing, and they weren't.

Comparative passages. The 2007 report gives a cause, blunt force injury, and a manner, homicide, without naming the instrument. Solberg keeps both and says the findings fit an object or a curb. The review spells out what the first report left open. It doesn't contradict it.

Tuesday Alma walked her grandmother in on her arm and sat down right behind her, and Consuelo Baca took the oath in a navy dress with a brooch at the collar and said I do like she'd been waiting since 2007 for somebody to ask.

Ana asked her what she saw. A man in a red jacket and a ball cap hit that man with something, and he went over backward on the curb, and the one in the cap ran. Ana asked about the face. I never saw a face. I said so then. Ana asked whether she'd heard anything earlier. A little boy crying for his papi. Ten to eleven, by my stove. I told the young officer. I told the detective. Nobody asked me again until her. She nodded at Dani, behind the rail.

Meredith stood up for one question. Mrs. Baca, you can't tell this court the man you saw wasn't Luis Ruiz. I can't tell you who he was. I never could. I told them that in 2007, and they wrote down the jacket.

Gene Vigil came up after her in a sport coat and nodded to Dani on his way past the rail. He testified the way a man reads his own report: the crew list, twenty one names, nobody on it interviewed but Luis Ruiz; the cap, written and struck; the scrapings, cancelled in November on his say. When Ana asked about the margin beside Consuelo's statement, he answered her looking at Teo. I wrote the word boy in that margin at nine in the morning, with a question mark. At three that afternoon I said excuse me, son, to a boy on the Ruiz basement stairs.

At eleven the State called Dani. She went up past her father without looking at him, which was the only way she could do it. Meredith asked her what she'd seen in the washer on the morning of October 28, 2007. My father's red work jacket. It was wet. Had she seen her father that night? No. I was at a sleepover in Thornton. Had the machine run? The cycle was done. It was wet. That's what I saw. Ana had no questions. Coming back down she looked at him, because now she could. Eleven minutes, start to finish, and nothing in it she hadn't said at fifteen, because it was all she'd ever seen.
At lunch, at a table in the cafeteria downstairs, Ana wrote her closing on one card and pushed it across.

Ana's closing, on one card. IN 2008 THE STATE SAID HE LIED ABOUT THE FIGHT, AND A MAN WHO LIES ABOUT A FIGHT IS HIDING A KILLING. HIS SON HAS TOLD THIS COURT HE HIT TRAVIS HENSLEY IN THAT LOT, AND HIS FATHER DROVE HIM AWAY. A FATHER WITH A TEN YEAR OLD WHO'D DONE THAT HAS A REASON TO LIE THAT ISN'T THE CURB. SO THE LIE DOESN'T POINT AT THE CURB.
Second sentence, Ana said, her pencil under HIS SON. Your brother hit him. What's it doing on my card?
It gives Pa's lie a reason that isn't the curb.

A reason to lie that isn't the curb. That's its whole job, Ana says. The State built on the lie. I'm not going to say he didn't lie. I'm going to hand them the reason. She underlines HIS SON once. The lie stays a lie. It just stops being evidence of the one thing the State used it for.

Role. The State used Luis's lie as a sign that he killed Travis. Teo's admission is a premise offering another explanation for the lie, a father protecting a son who'd hit a man. With that in place, the lie no longer supports the State's inference, which is the card's conclusion.

At two Ana stood up and said, The defense calls Luis Ruiz. Nobody had told Dani. She found out with the rest of the room. A deputy walked him from the table to the stand, and he took the oath with his hand flat, and sat, and laid both hands on the rail of the box where everybody could see them. She had the envelope in her bag. She didn't take it out.

Ana kept it short, and mostly she let him talk. I hit him first. In the bar. He had my boy by the arm, shaking him, and my boy's ten, he's been after me since Thursday about that game, and I hit the man before I thought about it. Ronnie put me out the back. The man came out after me and had me bent back over the tailgate of my truck and I couldn't get up. My son got the flashlight from behind the seat and hit him one time to get him off me. He looked at the judge. He was ten years old and that man had his father on a tailgate. That's why he swung. Nobody else can tell you that. I was the one under him. The man let go and walked off holding his face, he said, and he took his boy to his mother's in Globeville, and he never saw that man again.

She'd told him that on a jail phone Sunday night. He'd carried it up the three steps and put it down in front of a judge like it was his. In the second row Shannon Hensley's hands hadn't moved off the clasp of her purse.

Meredith let a few seconds go by before she stood up, and when she did she left her notes on the table. Had he told Detective Vigil he never touched anybody that night? Yes, ma'am, he had, and it was a lie. Had he told Vigil he drove home alone at a quarter to eleven? That was a lie too. Then why should this court believe a man who'd told the same two lies since 2007. I told them so nobody would come looking for my boy, he said. He's sitting right there. There's nobody left to look for.
He said it to Meredith and not to the room. Meredith wrote one word on her pad and said she had nothing further for this witness.
Ana's closing took twelve minutes, the card from lunch nearly word for word and then the left hand, with her reading glasses pushed up on her head the whole time. Meredith went second.

Nothing here proves anything, and Ms. Brennan has been careful never to say it does, she said. What we have is a second man who touched Travis Hensley at some point, in a bar with a hundred and twenty people in it on a World Series night. And we have a man who's believed for twenty years that he killed somebody, telling you a story nobody else in the world saw. Teo Ruiz loves his father. I believe that. A son would say anything to bring his father home, Judge, and we can't rely on a word of it.

A son would say anything. Meredith said it like it closed the subject, and Dani sat behind the rail with her bag on her knees trying to work out, in plain words, the way she would have on a Tuesday night with the practice book, what kind of argument that actually was.

It's an old one from her practice book. The dairy board paid the author, and a paid author writes anything, so throw the study out without reading it. A paid study can still be right. You'd have to open it to find out. Meredith had walked right past the cheek swab on July sixteenth to get to where she wanted to go.

Parallel flaw. Meredith goes from the witness's motive to rejecting everything he said, without weighing it against evidence like the sample he gave before he knew. The study argument makes the same move: the author has a reason to say it, so none of it can be believed.

It was ten to five when Meredith sat down. Esquibel took his glasses off and looked at nothing for a while, longer than Dani expected, and then he said he was taking it under advisement and both sides would get his ruling in writing, and thanked them, and the clerk said all rise, and everybody did.

The deputy came for her father at the side door. He stood, and he looked at the front row where Teo was for as long as the deputy let him, which wasn't long. Teo lifted one hand off his knee and put it back. Then the door shut.

In the hall the light came in sideways through the tall windows, and people stood around in it with nowhere to put their hands. Celeste Abeyta told Teo he'd done fine and shook his hand. Bianca had driven down at noon. She was at the far end by the drinking fountain, keys out. Ana was on the phone. Pencil behind her ear.
Shannon Hensley was the last one out. She stopped across the hall, ten feet off, maybe less, and looked at Dani, and kept on looking. She didn't say a word.
This time Dani didn't look at the floor.
Then Shannon took the stairs. Didn't wait on the elevator. Dani stayed put, bag on her shoulder, till the stairwell door had swung all the way shut.
